stories.title: The orphanage on the dunes
stories.teaser: In 1905 a purpose built brick home for children opened here, out among the sand dunes. Seven months later the 1906 earthquake wrecked it, yet every one of the 59 children inside got out unhurt. They camped on the dunes for twelve days.

photos.caption: The Nursery for Homeless Children on the north side of Lake Street between 14th and 15th Avenues

stories.verification_notes: Contemporary 1906 newspaper text on sfmuseum.org places the Nursery at Thirteenth Avenue and Lake Street, while later annual reports and the SF Story article say 14th Avenue. Treat 14th and Lake as correct, confirm on the Sanborn map.

stories.title: The orphanage that fell apart
stories.teaser: A few blocks east stood the Maria Kip Orphanage, which a 1906 report called the most complete ruin among the city's children's homes. All 125 children inside at the moment of the quake survived.

source.title: Every institution in the city for care of children damaged
source.author: 1906 newspaper account, transcribed
source.publisher: Museum of the City of San Francisco (sfmuseum.org)

photos.caption: The Maria Kip Orphanage, Lake Street near 7th Avenue, damaged after the 1906 earthquake
photos.credit: Harry O. Wood, Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley, BANC PIC 1957.007 Ser.1:115

stories.verification_notes: Claims come from the transcribed 1906 article; confirm the 125 figure and the building's later fate in a second source.

stories.title: The farm at the edge of the Presidio
stories.teaser: Before the avenues filled in, a small farm ran along the Presidio boundary here. The Bauchou family lived at 9 14th Avenue, and in 1905 they were the new orphanage's nearest neighbors, with Mountain Lake visible down the slope.

photos.caption: Bauchou home on 14th Avenue, view east toward Mountain Lake

stories.verification_notes: Image URL follows the OpenSFHistory pattern seen on other items; confirm it loads. OpenSFHistory caption names Bernard Bauchou as the occupant of 9 14th Avenue.

stories.title: The streetcar graveyard
stories.teaser: This whole block between Irving, Lincoln Way, 14th and Funston was once a yard where retired streetcars waited for the scrapper, among the sand of the Sunset. It was planned as a carhouse in 1907 and later served Muni as a storage lot.

photos.caption: Aerial view of the Market Street Railway boneyard, looking west on Irving at 14th Avenue
photos.credit: via SFMTA blog; original source to confirm

stories.verification_notes: The SFMTA post points to a Western Neighborhoods Project article and podcast episode 182 for more; find that WNP page and make it the primary source.

stories.title: Many lives of a corner
stories.teaser: In the early 1970s the southeast corner of Ninth and Irving held a bar called The Stein, also known as Mac's Place, served by green streetcars. A Jamba Juice came later, and a French chicken sandwich restaurant was announced for the space in 2025.

source.title: Then and Now: Ninth Avenue and Irving Street
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Mac's Place, The Stein, on the southeast corner of Ninth Avenue and Irving Street (postcard)
photos.credit: Private collector / Western Neighborhoods Project / OpenSFHistory
